extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and journalists interested in wartime British newspaper practices
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporary newspaper reporting and editorial/production practices for British papers during World War II, including space quotas, content-prioritization, material restrictions and distribution practices driven by shortages and censorship. The page is a collection of wartime news articles and descriptive commentary about how British newspapers were produced and what they contained under wartime constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisement space quotas
rubrics_metrics.description: Morning papers are permitted to use 40 per cent of their space for advertisements, afternoon 45 per cent and weeklies 55 per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: "Morning papers are permitted to use 40 per cent of their space for advertisements, afternoon 45 per cent_and weeklies 55 per cent." (used as formal limits on ad content in papers during the period).

rubrics_metrics.name: Front pages devoted to war (front-page editorial policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The papers themselves for the most part have given over the front pages to the war — only the staid Times fills that page with advertisements after the old British newspaper practice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/implication: Front pages should prioritize war coverage; filling front page with advertisements is the exception (the Times) rather than the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage prioritization under newsprint shortage
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sports news sections can be covered with the average outspread hand. Important financial and business news is retained. Crime is cut to a few sentences. Court cases rate only a sentence, usually a bright comment of the magistrate or of a witness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit editorial prioritization: retain crucial business/financial reporting; significantly truncate sports, crime, and court reporting to conserve space. Examples given (few sentences for crime; one-sentence court reports often a pithy quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material constraint: use of thinner paper
rubrics_metrics.description: "Now, in a new form of curtailment, thinner paper has been decreed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production/material standard imposed to conserve newsprint; implies changes to layout and legibility trade-offs for all editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution constraint: home delivery limits and encouraged sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person has to put his name on a long waiting list to apply for a home delivered paper, and when he finally gets one will be asked to pass it along to his neighbor after he reads it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational policy for scarce home delivery: restricted subscriptions with informal circulation/sharing etiquette to extend limited copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-format constraints and small-form inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of reduced/condensed content formats: "In the Express, there is a miniature crossword puzzle, and a children's story in 14 lines. Comic strips never caught on Britain, although small cartoons are common."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial choices favor very short features (e.g., 14-line children's story, miniature puzzles) and small cartoons instead of full comic strips to save space while retaining light content.
